comparator.name: Economics and Business Economics (Economie en Bedrijfseconomie)
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 Economics track totals 180 EC: ten compulsory 6 EC courses in each of Years 1 and 2, 30 EC open study, three compulsory 6 EC final-year subjects and a 12 EC Economics thesis. Economics is the first-listed broad track in the official schedule, selected neutrally before UCR construction; Accounting, Finance and Marketing belong to the separate Business Economics track and are not mixed into this comparator. English teaching has Dutch tutorial, expression and exam-answer options in Years 1–2; Year 3 is English. BSA normally requires 42 first-year EC and a pass in QRM I. The English diagnostic or completed refresher gates the Academic Skills grade. Zero-credit SAM provides mentor meetings each period, not added EC. The second-year Research Paper is a three-student project with data/model-based inquiry, paper, referee report and presentations; QRM I/II and Academic Skills are recommended background. Thesis entry at application requires 120 EC including QRM II, the entire first year, and at most two outstanding Year-2 courses. It is individual literature-review or empirical/theoretical economic research with thesis and video presentation; apply early October for periods 2–3 or late February for periods 5–6. These relative deadlines are not imposed as dated future-cohort deadlines. Open study normally requires 90 EC, at most 6 EC level 100, at least 12 EC level 300, no compulsory overlap and prior examination-board approval except SBE faculty, university or Education minors. Business Administration and Economics university minors are prohibited for EBE. Course manuals may require attendance; the Ethics tutorials and two online meetings are compulsory. Honours is additional. The main annual chart shows thesis12EC, but the specialisation subtable incorrectly prints6EC; the exact annual thesis catalogue independently confirms12EC. Retain12EC, not an invented extra unit or guessed two-part6EC allocation. Hidden duplicate text in the main chart is not an additional Macroeconomics course.

routeSelection.basis: The generic normalized programme has an Economics track and a Business Economics track with Accounting, Finance or Marketing specialization. Neither overarching track is a clear proxy for the entire degree; Economics is the first track in the 2026–27 official annual schedule, so the neutral official-order rule fixes it before considering UCR offerings. The Business Economics specializations remain candidate related directions.

core: Microeconomics and consumer, firm and market decisions
Macroeconomics, international economic events and policy
Public economics, labour, development, inequality and broad prosperity
Quantitative economics: mathematics, statistics, programming and introductory econometrics
Accounting, finance, marketing and organisational foundations in the shared first year
Economic ethics, sustainable growth and environmental choices
Economic research, writing, thesis and advice to public and private actors
adjacent: Business Economics Finance specialization and banking or investment decisions
Business Economics Marketing specialization and consumer engagement
questions: How do economic policies affect labour markets, inequality and broad prosperity?
How can banks manage risk and remain financially stable?
How do consumers respond to marketing and firm decisions?
Can energy choices such as nuclear power address climate change sustainably?

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
trace: Mandatory Year-1 personal/professional development and academic skills.
Financial statements and annual-report analysis explain firm information used in economic and business decisions; not a substitute for CAPM, portfolio pricing or advanced corporate finance.
AI business cases analyse effects on competition, labour, growth, inequality and corporate governance; an economic application, not a technical AI-methods course.
Applied budgeting, investment and risk decisions add a financial-decision application to macroeconomic and firm analysis; no dedicated asset-pricing or financial-stability sequence is claimed.
Supply/demand, consumer and firm theory, market structures and short-run macroeconomics establish economic foundations.
Growth, inflation, unemployment, fiscal/monetary policy, business cycles and trade support economic-policy analysis; not a duplicate of VU’s specialised intermediate policy course.
Uncertainty, behavioural preferences, imperfect competition, factor markets, equilibrium and externalities implement intermediate microeconomic analysis after statistical foundations.
Market failure, public goods, taxation, spending and redistribution directly implement public-welfare and policy analysis.
OLS/GLS/instrumental variables, sampling distributions, tests and an empirical economic paper provide applied econometric research; VU Probit/panel/time-series coverage is not assumed.
Experiments, biases, heuristics and framing explain deviations from conventional economic choice and support consumer or policy interpretation.
Customer interviews, needs-to-product translation, cost/proceeds and sustainable prototypes implement consumer-led market validation, not generic design breadth.
Consumer psychology, brand trust, marketing plans and strategy implement the evidenced consumer/marketing direction.
Business-model analysis, digital-value opportunities and a strategic plan implement responsible digital business strategy.
Collecting and analysing customer evidence and communicating findings provide market-research practice complementary to econometric methods.
Institutional, political and cultural forces, trade and corporate responsibility explain the conditions under which firms make cross-border economic decisions.
Venture ideation, customer validation and business planning implement the target’s entrepreneurship and firm-decision strand.
Operationalisation, sampling, experimental design, inference, ANOVA and a group project establish empirical research before Microeconomics and advanced work.
Motivation, decision making, leadership, group dynamics and organisational structure explain workplace behaviour; not formal organisational economics.
BATNA/ZOPA, bargaining, trade-offs and simulations implement consumer/business negotiation and strategic interpersonal decisions, not market-equilibrium theory.
Data cleaning, visualisation and manipulation support reproducible economic/consumer evidence and project work.
Regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, trees and clustering support predictive analysis of economic/consumer data; causal inference remains the econometrics contribution.
Python programming and debugging implement computational tools for digital business and empirical projects.
Calculus, integration and differential equations give mathematical tools for economic modelling; no unsupported linear-algebra/linear-programming claim.
Numerical roots, interpolation, differentiation/integration and differential equations support quantitative model solution; not a dedicated optimisation course.
Probability distributions, estimation, sampling and simulation provide a mathematical basis for empirical economic inference.
Physical climate drivers, social impacts, mitigation and adaptation constrain economic climate-policy choices; not an environmental/transport-economics replacement.
Moral theories and applied equality, future-generation and climate questions support evaluation of welfare-policy judgments; not VU’s dedicated corporate/market-ethics scope.
EU institutions, legislative dossiers, interest groups and transparency data explain the political institutions shaping economic policy, not technical economic-policy models.

alternatives.label: Economics, public policy and sustainable prosperity
alternatives.concept: Economic theory and empirical methods organise the study of public policy, welfare, financial decisions and sustainable prosperity. Microeconomics, international macroeconomics, public economics, behavioral economics and applied econometrics provide the substantive economic response. Climate science, ethics, institutional governance and firm-level decisions make specific complements; they do not replace VU’s specialist development, regional/transport, human-capital and economic-policy courses or thesis.
alternatives.labelReason: Public Economics, macroeconomics, sustainability and ethical reasoning organize the Economics-track comparison.

alternatives.label: Consumer evidence, marketing and digital business
alternatives.concept: Economic and statistical foundations lead into consumer evidence, marketing plans, product validation, negotiation and responsible digital business strategy. This is a different application of economics and empirical methods from the public-policy option, supported by the target’s Marketing direction. It does not reproduce VU’s full specialist marketing or compulsory thesis sequence.

alternatives.distinctness: Four courses/30EC differ on each side. Programming, Consumer Product Design, Negotiation and Digital Strategy replace Public Economics, Climate Change, Ethics and Money/Banking. The consumer option prioritises customer investigation and business strategy; the primary option prioritises public welfare, sustainability and financial decisions. Programming enables its digital/data implementation; no arbitrary substitutions are used.

candidates.label: Marketing specialization, consumer behaviour and innovation

selection.assessment: Retain two qualified responses: an economics/public-policy programme and a distinct consumer/marketing application. The Finance candidate has genuine financial-decision and business-law contributions, but one7.5ECbanking/finance course and accounting, generic discrete/linear mathematics and governance do not implement its advertised specialised investment/financial-stability progression. No distinct full finance alternative is established. Accounting lacks an advanced accounting/information-systems sequence. Nuclear energy is a single illustrative climate-policy question, not a stable independent academic direction; its broader sustainability issue belongs to the primary option. No third alternative is manufactured.

notes.text: The UCR options provide economic theory, quantitative and applied econometric methods, and either public-policy or consumer/business applications. They do not reproduce VU’s dedicated development, spatial/transport, human-capital and economic-policy sequence, specialist business-economics routes or compulsory Economics thesis. Accounting concerns financial statements; general mathematics and governance do not establish a specialist Finance programme. No degree equivalence or automatic master’s eligibility is implied.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Economics and Business Economics studies decisions by people, firms and governments through economic theory, quantitative methods and research. After common first-year study, students choose Economics or Business Economics, with Accounting, Finance and Marketing specialisations in the latter.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Two qualified UCR alternatives retain substantial economic theory and empirical methods. One emphasises public welfare, sustainability and financial decisions; the other emphasises consumer evidence, marketing and digital business. Their specific complementary courses do not replace the full specialist VU sequence or compulsory thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The selected Economics pathway contains 180 EC, including 30 EC open study and a 12 EC individual thesis. Thesis entry requires 120 EC including QRM II, all first-year courses and at most two remaining second-year courses. The English diagnostic or refresher gates Academic Skills; zero-credit SAM mentoring is separate. The minor has level, approval and nonoverlap conditions; Economics and Business Administration university minors are prohibited.
